source: Johnson & Goldstein (2003) Do defaults save lives? Science
finding: Online experiment: the default option changed stated organ donation. Opt-out and neutral framing gave about the same high rate. Only opt-in (the US practice) was low.
numbers: N=161 respondents, three conditions. Consent: opt-in 42%, opt-out 82%, neutral (forced choice, no default) 79%. Opt-out not significantly different from neutral.
limits: Hypothetical choice, not actual donation. Opt-in was the odd one out, so the harm is in the opt-in default more than the benefit of opt-out.
agent_relevance: A default can be a hidden anchor. Compare it with a no-default (forced choice) condition to see which direction the bias runs.

source: Johnson & Goldstein (2003) Do defaults save lives? Science (country data)
finding: Across European countries, presumed-consent (opt-out) countries had far higher effective consent than explicit-consent (opt-in) countries.
numbers: Explicit consent: Denmark 4.25%, Netherlands 27.5%, UK 17.17%, Germany 12%. Presumed consent: Austria 99.98%, Belgium 98%, France 99.91%, Hungary 99.97%, Poland 99.5%, Portugal 99.64%, Sweden 85.9%. The paper also reports a 16.3% increase (P<0.02) in donation rate in a cross-country analysis (exact model not checked).
limits: Correlational, 11 countries. Effective consent is not actual transplants; later critics note infrastructure and family consent matter (from memory, not opened).
agent_relevance: The structure of the question, not its content, moves the answer. Our S0 gate should not let the way a prompt is posed set the verdict.

source: Johnson & Goldstein (2003) Do defaults save lives? Science (three explanations)
finding: Three named mechanisms for default effects: defaults read as policy-maker advice, accepting a default is effortless, and the default is the status quo so changing it feels like a loss. Authors argue preferences are constructed, not stored.
numbers: A mouse-click change in the online study largely removed the effort explanation, yet the default effect stayed large (82% vs 42%).
limits: Mechanism evidence is indirect. Later work (Jachimowicz et al. 2019, not opened) separates the three.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the advice and effort routes both apply: a stated or implied answer in the prompt is read as a recommendation (see G4, G5 in the schema).

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: a meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions. PNAS
finding: Large meta-analysis of choice architecture (nudge) studies found a small to medium average effect.
numbers: 214 publications, 455 effect sizes, 2,149,683 participants. Overall Cohen d = 0.45, 95% CI [0.39, 0.52]; without influential outliers d = 0.42 [0.37, 0.46].
quote: choice architecture interventions overall promote behavior change with a small to medium effect size
limits: Headline is not corrected for publication bias. Mostly short-term behaviour.
agent_relevance: Treat any single published nudge effect as an upper bound.

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: a meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions. PNAS (by category)
finding: Structure-changing nudges (defaults, effort, ordering) beat information nudges and assistance nudges.
numbers: Decision structure k=227, d=0.55 [0.45,0.64]. Decision information k=130, d=0.38 [0.29,0.47]. Decision assistance k=98, d=0.31 [0.23,0.39]. Structure significantly larger than the other two; information and assistance did not differ.
limits: Categories are the authors own taxonomy.
agent_relevance: Debiasing by structure beats debiasing by telling. For the agent: change the procedure (forced base-rate step, order, defaults) rather than adding reminders.

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: a meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions. PNAS (by domain)
finding: Effect size depends strongly on behavioural domain.
limits: Food effects up to 2.5 times other domains; food is also where publication bias was weakest in the reanalysis.
agent_relevance: Domain matters: a debiasing step tuned on one task type may not transfer to another.

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: a meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions. PNAS (heterogeneity and bias)
finding: Effects vary hugely between studies, and the funnel shows positive-result bias.
numbers: I2 = 99.67%, tau2 = 0.23, 95% prediction interval [-0.48, 1.39]; authors estimate about 15% of interventions could backfire. Egger b = 2.28, P<0.001. Moderate-bias adjustment gives d = 0.31; severe-bias adjustment gives d = 0.03. Lab, artifactual, framed and natural field experiments did not differ (P = 0.846).
limits: The authors used a selection-model sensitivity check, not a full bias-corrected fit; Maier et al. went further.
agent_relevance: Any structural debiaser needs a measured per-task effect on our own items, including the chance that it hurts.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias. PNAS
finding: Reanalysis of the Mertens data with robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA with selection models plus PET-PEESE) removed almost all of the average effect.
numbers: Unadjusted random effects d = 0.43 [0.38, 0.48]. RoBMA-PSMA ignoring clustering d = 0.04 [0.00, 0.14]. RoBMA-PSMA using the most precise estimate per study d = 0.11 [0.00, 0.24].
limits: The page I read labelled the Bayes factors inconsistently and did not give inclusion Bayes factors; check the OSF repository before citing them. Bias correction can over-correct under heavy heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on aggregate nudge claims; test on our own tasks with held-out items (G3).

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias. PNAS (bias by subdomain)
finding: Strong evidence of publication bias in nearly all subdomains. Food was the exception.
numbers: Bayes factor for publication bias BFpb > 10 across subdomains except food (BFpb = 2.49 with most precise estimates). Heterogeneity evidence in all categories and domains except finance.
limits: Absence of evidence for an effect is not evidence of no effect; some subdomains may hold real effects (replies by Mertens et al. and Szaszi et al. argue this; not opened).
agent_relevance: Keep structural nudges that have a mechanism and a measured effect on our items; drop those that rest on literature averages.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) RCTs to scale: comprehensive evidence from two nudge units. Econometrica
finding: All trials from two large US nudge units gave effects far smaller than nudge studies published in academic journals.
numbers: 126 RCTs, about 23 million people. Nudge units: 1.4 percentage points (8.0% over control mean). Academic journal nudges: 8.7 percentage points (33.4% over control mean).
limits: Read from the journal abstract page, not the full paper. Topics and behavioural channels differ between the two sets.
agent_relevance: Expected real-world gain is roughly one sixth of the published figure. Plan for shrinkage when we move from a pilot to a benchmark.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) RCTs to scale: comprehensive evidence from two nudge units. Econometrica (why the gap)
finding: The authors attribute the gap mainly to selective publication together with low power in academic studies, and the rest to differences in topic and channel.
numbers: Selective publication plus low power explains about 70% of the gap, per the abstract page.
limits: Decomposition is model dependent.
agent_relevance: Report all runs, including nulls, in our own logs.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3)
finding: Cost and demand forecasts for large projects are biased, not just noisy, and have not improved over decades. Technical explanations (bad data or models) fail the test; optimism and strategic misrepresentation fit.
numbers: Mean cost overrun in constant prices: rail 44.7%, bridges and tunnels 33.8%, roads 20.4%. Rail passenger forecast error -51.4% on average, 84% of rail projects wrong by more than 20%. Road traffic error 9.5% average, half wrong by more than 20%. No improvement over 70 years (cost) or 30 years (demand).
limits: Transport infrastructure data, mostly European. Reference classes are coarse.
agent_relevance: Split our own estimate errors into bias (fix with class record) and noise (fix with averaging).

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3) (method)
finding: Reference class forecasting has three steps: pick a reference class of similar past projects, build the outcome distribution for the class, place the current project in it. It does not forecast specific events.
numbers: Steps: (1) identify the class, (2) establish the probability distribution, (3) compare the project with the distribution. Built on Kahneman and Tversky outside view and the planning fallacy.
limits: Choosing the class is the hard part. Lower uplifts only if the project is clearly better than the class.
agent_relevance: This is the S0 gate/S7 selection rule we want: a base rate from the class record before the inside-view story.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3) (uplifts)
finding: The UK Department for Transport turned the distributions into budget uplifts by acceptable risk of overrun.
numbers: Road: 15% uplift for 50% risk of overrun, 45% for 10% risk. Rail: 40% for 50% risk, 68% for 10% risk. At 80% certainty to stay in budget: rail 57%, roads 32%. Uplift rises as acceptable risk falls.
limits: Uplifts are for capital cost in constant prices in one data period.
agent_relevance: A direct template: choose a risk level, read the quantile from the class record, apply it in code (G5).

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3) (Kahneman curriculum story)
finding: Kahneman Israeli curriculum team: inside-view estimates were 18 to 30 months. The expert recall of similar projects gave a very different answer.
numbers: Team estimates 18-30 months. Expert: about 40% of comparable teams never finished; none of the finishers took under 7 or over 10 years. Actual completion after 8 years, curriculum rarely used.
limits: One anecdote retold from Lovallo and Kahneman (2003), not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: The inside view ignored a 40% failure rate. The S0 gate should ask for the failure rate of the class first.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3) (outside-view test)
finding: A simple prompt to consider relevant outside-view information before the forecast reduced overconfidence but did not remove it.
numbers: Students expected to beat 84% of peers (impossible). A second group, first asked about entrance scores and peers scores, lowered the expected rating by 20%. Still overconfident.
limits: Retold from Lovallo and Kahneman (2003); original sample sizes not given here.
agent_relevance: A fixed step that pulls class data in first helps, but is not enough alone.

source: Lerner & Tetlock (1999) Accounting for the effects of accountability. Psychological Bulletin 125
finding: Accountability (having to justify judgments to an audience) helps only under conditions: the audience views are unknown, accountability comes before the judgment, and the audience wants accuracy. Otherwise people conform or become defensive.
numbers: Not opened this session; from memory. No figures recorded.
limits: Not verified from the text. Check the conditions before use.
agent_relevance: Self-critique should be pre-decisional and see no preferred answer (matches G5: the judge sees no proposed answer).

source: Camerer & Hogarth (1999) The effects of financial incentives in experiments: a review and capital-labor-production framework. J Risk and Uncertainty 19
finding: Review of experiments with and without financial incentives. Incentives help when extra effort pays off in the task, and often do not remove well-known judgment anomalies.
numbers: Not opened; from memory, about 74 papers reviewed. Exact counts not checked.
limits: Not verified from the text.
agent_relevance: Money-like text in a prompt is unlikely to fix reasoning bias; tasks need a structure that makes effort useful.

source: Madrian & Shea (2001) The power of suggestion: inertia in 401(k) participation. QJE 116
finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation sharply for new hires at one US company.
numbers: Not opened; from memory, participation about 37% before vs about 86% after, but many stayed at the default savings rate.
limits: Not verified here. Default sticking also caused harm when the default contribution was low.
agent_relevance: Defaults stick even when not best. An agent default (first answer, first option) will stick too.

source: Thaler & Sunstein (2008) Nudge: improving decisions about health, wealth and happiness
finding: Defines a nudge as a change in choice architecture that alters behaviour predictably without forbidding options or changing incentives much (libertarian paternalism).
numbers: Not opened. Definition only.
limits: The definition excludes bans and large incentives, so it is not equal to every structural debiaser.
agent_relevance: The scaffold is choice architecture for the model: it sets order, defaults and framing, in code.

source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994) Exploring the planning fallacy. JPSP 67
finding: Students predicted thesis completion times that were too early. Asking for a past record did not remove the bias fully.
numbers: Not opened; from memory, average prediction about 34 days vs about 56 days actual, about 30% finished by the predicted date. Check before citing.
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Base-rate use fails when the inside view is vivid; the step must be forced and the record shown.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases. NeurIPS
finding: Codex and CodeGen are hurt by framing and anchoring-like irrelevant context, and copy it into the output.
numbers: Irrelevant preceding functions lowered Codex accuracy by 22.3 to 30.5 points. Availability-style test: accuracy fell from 50% to 17% when operation order flipped. Conflicting function name: Codex accuracy 100% down to 4.4-4.6%. Codex erroneously deleted files on at least 80% of prompts with three or more package imports.
limits: Code models from 2021-22. Small tests for GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Prompt context acts as an anchor. Anything placed before the question, such as a draft answer, will pull the output.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) (GPT-3 anchoring replication)
finding: GPT-3 estimates moved toward anchors in a replication of Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) with anchors built from the true answer.
numbers: 14 of the original 15 questions; anchors set 20% and 50% above or below the true answer; the paper tabulates how often the estimate shifts toward the anchor.
limits: Small sample, template prompts, on average 41% of outputs were gibberish.
agent_relevance: Test our own agent for anchor pull from drafts and prior answers.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed anchoring, the conjunction fallacy, a framing effect and an endowment effect, like human participants.
numbers: Anchoring (30 trials per condition): low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.5 (humans, N=60 total); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.50; t(58)=8.78 for ChatGPT. Conjunction: ChatGPT chose it 18/20, humans 10/20. Endowment: ChatGPT kept the owned coin 85% (CI 70.1-94.3).
limits: Small cells, GPT-3.5. Prompts needed a pretend-to-be-an-agent line to avoid refusals.
agent_relevance: The model carries the biases that debiasing targets, so structure must come from outside the model.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large language models understand and can be enhanced by emotional stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Adding emotional or stakes statements to the prompt raised scores across models. This is the closest LLM analogue of an incentive.
numbers: 45 tasks (24 Instruction Induction, 21 BIG-Bench), six LLMs including ChatGPT, GPT-4, Llama 2. Relative gain 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench; human study with 106 participants: 10.9% mean gain on performance, truthfulness, responsibility.
quote: LLMs possess emotional intelligence and can be enhanced by emotional stimuli
limits: The 115% is relative to a low base. Effects vary by model and task; replication on strong models not checked here.
agent_relevance: Cheap but unreliable. Use only if measured on our items; never as a gate.

source: Bsharat, Myrzakhan & Shen (2023) Principled instructions are all you need (26 prompt principles)
finding: Lists 26 prompt principles, including an incentive (tip $xxx for a better solution) and a penalty (You will be penalized).
numbers: ATLAS benchmark: average gain of 57.7% in quality and 36.4% in correctness for GPT-4; gains grow with model size (over 20% more from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4). Tip and penalty are two of the 26; per-principle numbers are in figures I did not read.
limits: Hand-built benchmark, few questions per principle, no significance tests seen.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for money-style incentives in prompts. Keep them out of the schema unless our bench shows gains.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: A dataset of 13,465 prompts tests prompt-induced, sequential and inherent bias in admissions decisions. Awareness, contrastive and counterfactual prompts gave small or inconsistent gains. Self-help (the model rewrites its own prompt to remove the bias cue) worked best on large models.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help left biased prompts at 17.2% (framing) and 8.5% (status quo) in one model; high-capacity models cut bias cues to 0 for group attribution and framing.
limits: Admissions task only. Few-shot and counterfactual prompts sometimes broke the model (admit or reject nearly everything). Low-capacity models changed 40-52% of decisions in anchoring self-help.
agent_relevance: Structural fix beats instruction: remove the cue in a separate call, then decide on the clean version.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) (primacy bias)
finding: Strong primacy: options A and B chosen more often than C and D when all were equally likely. Awareness helps a little. Self-help gives the most balanced spread.
numbers: Reported as distributions in a figure; no single number.
limits: Figure only.
agent_relevance: Shuffle option order in code and vote over orders (a code-side structural fix).

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Zero-shot LLMs forecast poorly. A retrieval plus scratchpad system, which asks the model to weigh arguments and to check for over- or under-confidence and consider historical base rates, nears the human crowd.
numbers: Dataset: 48,754 questions, 33,664 binary, 7,174,607 human forecasts from 5 platforms; test set after June 2023. Brier: random 0.250; best base model GPT-4-1106 0.208; human crowd 0.149; system 0.179 (accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%). Averaging system and crowd was best in every setting.
limits: The base-rate step is one of several prompt parts; no ablation of it alone was read. The system beat the crowd only in selective settings.
agent_relevance: Base-rate prompting is already used in forecasting pipelines. In our scaffold, supply base rates from stored class records, not model recall.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) (baseline calibration)
finding: Most pre-trained models scored near or worse than the unskilled 0.5 forecast out of the box.
numbers: Only GPT-4 and Claude-2 series beat the 0.25 Brier baseline by more than 0.02. The optimized system was well calibrated on validation and test.
limits: Time-series data; the paper says standard errors likely understate the true error.
agent_relevance: Without structure the model has no usable base-rate sense. Hand it the class record.
